Q168.L1t: Alice in Wonderland is a children's story in which Alice repeatedly changes size after eating or drinking strange things.
Q168.L2t: In this scene Alice enters the Rabbit's little house, finds a fan and gloves upstairs, and then drinks from a bottle near the looking-glass.
Q168.L3t: The passage says Alice was so much frightened that she ran off at once in the direction the Rabbit pointed to, right after he called out to her.
Q168.L4t: Alice felt fear when the Rabbit shouted at her to run home and fetch his gloves and fan.
Q168.L2f: The bottle Alice drank from in the Rabbit's house was sealed with wax and had a long printed warning on its label.
Q168.L3f: The passage says that once Alice stopped growing she was relieved, because her arm and foot were free and she could move around the room easily.
Q168.L4f: Alice felt comfortable once she stopped growing and found the cramped room pleasant.

Q169.L1t: The passage is about how clothing works as a form of communication and reflects people's values in society.
Q169.L2t: A researcher in Michigan studied how white collar and blue collar workers viewed dress as early as 1955.
Q169.L3t: The passage says blue collar workers were less aware of being judged by clothes, but recognized that any departure from the accepted pattern of dress would be made fun of by fellow workers.
Q169.L4t: Blue collar workers care about their clothes because they do not want to be laughed at by their coworkers.
Q169.L2f: The Michigan researcher in 1955 found that blue collar workers paid more attention to dress than white collar workers did.
Q169.L3f: The passage says blue collar workers were fully and clearly aware that others would judge them by their clothing, and this awareness shaped how they dressed.
Q169.L4f: Blue collar workers pay attention to their clothes because they know very clearly that people will judge them on that basis.

Q170.L1t: The passage is a personal book recommendation about a classic work of American fiction.
Q170.L2t: The writer describes the plot, scenes and characters of The Adventure of Tom Sawyer and mentions that Twain wrote it in 1876.
Q170.L3t: The passage ends with a direct instruction to the reader, "Go on--- read it!", along with the writer's hope that the reader will enjoy it too.
Q170.L4t: The writer writes the article to encourage readers to go and read the book.
Q170.L2f: Twain wrote The Adventure of Tom Sawyer in formal British English, which is why many readers find it hard to follow.
Q170.L3f: The passage's main stated purpose is to explain its language, saying the book sounds real because it is in everyday southern English, and the rest only supports this point.
Q170.L4f: The writer writes the article to explain why the story sounds so real to readers.
